1: Programme context: Strategy2Results®. Collective Intelligence for Execution. Where Strategy Meets the People Who Execute It.

What Strategy2Results® is: Strategy2Results® is a structured leadership certification programme designed to equip senior leaders with the behavioural intelligence, cross-functional perspective, and execution discipline to translate strategic intent into measurable organisational results, consistently and collectively.

The programme is underpinned by three integrated pillars, Direction, Influence, and Grounding (DIG), each building on the last to produce a leader who understands strategy and actively integrates it across the enterprise.
“The quality of your strategy is a direct function of the quality of the thinking environment in which it was made. Strategy2Results® is designed to build that environment, deliberately.”
The certification, what participants earn: CESI, Certified Enterprise Strategy Integrator.

What the title means: The designation Certified Enterprise Strategy Integrator recognises leaders who have demonstrated the capacity to operate beyond the boundaries of their own function: to see the enterprise whole, to integrate competing priorities into coherent direction, and to create the conditions in which strategy moves from intent to execution. It is a practice credential, earned through application, peer challenge, and demonstrated integration across the four pillars of the programme.
What CESI holders are equipped to do:
- Navigate strategic decisions through multiple executive perspectives simultaneously.
- Identify and interrupt cognitive bias at the point of decision.
- Translate enterprise strategy into executable, cross-functional priority frameworks.
- Build and sustain leadership cultures where honest challenge and collective intelligence are the norm.
- Hold their own function accountable to enterprise outcomes.
- Diagnose execution failure at its source: thinking, alignment, and process.

Programme architecture at a glance: The Strategy2Results® programme is structured across four modules, each representing a pillar of enterprise strategy integration: Module 1 · Foundation (Behavioural Strategy Fundamentals), Module 2 · Direction (Pillar 1), Module 3 · Influence (Pillar 2) and Module 4 · Grounding (Pillar 3). The Foundation module is the prerequisite for all that follows: it establishes the behavioural and cognitive literacy that every subsequent unit requires.

Unit 1 in six sections: Section 1 · Orientation (Introduction: Understanding the Basics); Section 2 · Awareness (What Behavioural Strategy Is); Section 3 · Intelligence (Why Behavioural Strategy Is Critical); Section 4 · Extrapolating (Where Behavioural Strategy Operates); Section 5 · Integration (How to Build Collective Intelligence); Section 6 · Application (the unit in practice).

Who the programme is for: Strategy2Results® is designed for senior leaders who carry enterprise-level responsibility, whether they hold a CXO title or a role that functions at that level. It is for leaders who are already capable within their function and who are ready for the next level of challenge: leading at the level of the whole.
The programme is particularly valuable for:
- Executive Team Members: CXO leaders who need to align across functions and translate board-level strategy into enterprise execution.
- Senior Leaders on the Rise: high-potential leaders preparing for executive roles who need to develop enterprise-wide perspective before stepping into it.
- Strategy & Governance Teams: leaders responsible for planning, strategy office, or enterprise performance who need the tools to drive integration and execution quality.
Strategy2Results® is a practice you develop, and a capability your organisation keeps.
4: The problem this programme solves: Research consistently shows that 60–90% of strategies fail in delivery. The causes are behavioural, structural, and entirely predictable.
The pattern, what it costs, and what S2R® builds:

- Leaders think in functional silos. What it costs: fragmented execution, misaligned KPIs, teams rowing in different directions. What S2R® builds: an enterprise-wide perspective, the capacity to think from every seat at the table.

- Cognitive bias distorts decisions invisibly. What it costs: poor capital allocation, strategic inertia, innovation suppression, purpose drift. What S2R® builds: behavioural intelligence, the skill of catching bias before it becomes a cost.

- Strategy is cascaded without being integrated. What it costs: execution energy dissipates as direction moves down the organisation. What S2R® builds: integration discipline, the ability to connect intent to action across all functions.

- Emotional climate is left unmanaged. What it costs: fear and ego replace curiosity; honest challenge disappears; groupthink fills the gap. What S2R® builds: climate leadership, the deliberate creation of the conditions where quality thinking happens.

- Accountability is structural and has yet to become cultural. What it costs: progress is reported without being owned; strategy reviews become performance theatre. What S2R® builds: a culture of strategic ownership, where leaders carry the whole as well as their part.
The Executive Leadership Perspective Simulation: The most powerful feature of the Strategy2Results® programme is how participants learn.

In every session, participants are assigned an executive role outside their own function (CEO, CFO, COO, CHRO, CTO, CMO, CCO, CPO, CRO, or CSO) and required to analyse each unit’s challenge through that executive’s priorities, concerns, and strategic perspective. Facilitators actively enforce this role discipline. It is not optional and it is not light-touch.

This is the mechanism through which the programme builds collective intelligence. By inhabiting another executive’s perspective with rigour, as a genuine analytical discipline, participants develop the capacity to anticipate cross-functional implications, surface hidden dependencies, and make decisions that hold at the enterprise level as well as within their own function.

“This is what separates strategic leaders from functional experts: the ability to think from a seat you do not occupy, and to do it well enough that the person who does occupy it trusts your reasoning.”
The Strategy2Results® Leadership Matrix: the ten CXO roles used throughout the programme, their functional equivalents, and the primary strategic perspective each brings to execution.
- CEO (Managing Director / President / Executive Director / Founder): enterprise direction, stakeholder credibility, strategic coherence across all functions.
- CFO (Finance Director / Head of Finance): capital allocation, financial risk discipline, return logic and investment prioritisation.
- COO (Operations Director / Head of Operations): operational flow, execution reliability, cross-functional coordination and delivery rhythm.
- CHRO (HR Director / Head of HR / People & Culture Director): people capacity, culture coherence, leadership capability and change readiness.
- CTO (IT Director / Head of Technology): technology architecture, digital capability, systems integration and innovation velocity.
- CMO (Marketing Director / Head of Marketing): customer insight, brand positioning, market relevance and commercial storytelling.
- CCO (Commercial Director / Head of Sales & Business Development): revenue generation, commercial partnerships, customer acquisition and retention logic.
- CPO (Procurement Director / Supply Chain Director): supply chain integrity, procurement risk, sourcing discipline and cost optimisation.
- CRO (Risk & Compliance Director / Head of Risk): risk appetite, regulatory compliance, governance frameworks and enterprise resilience.
- CSO (Strategy Director / Head of Strategy): strategic architecture, planning cycles, cross-functional strategic coherence.
6: The 4-Point Learning Arc (the logic behind the sections): Every session in the Strategy2Results® programme is structured around a four-stage learning arc: a disciplined sequence that moves participants from conceptual understanding through to executive application. The arc is a cognitive scaffold, designed to ensure that each unit is learned, internalised and pressure-tested.

AWARENESS (What · Interrogative Anchor): What is this unit? What are its core concepts? What terrain are we entering? Every session opens by establishing a precise shared understanding of the unit under examination. Participants are oriented to definitions and to the strategic terrain the unit governs: the patterns it reveals, the failures it explains, and the language that makes it navigable. Awareness is the foundation without which intelligence has nothing to interrogate.

INTELLIGENCE (Why · Ignition Point): Why does this unit matter for strategy execution? What is the business case and evidence? Once the terrain is mapped, the session builds the case for why this unit is not optional. Research, organisational evidence, and real-world failure patterns are used to demonstrate the cost of ignoring what the unit reveals. Intelligence is the stage that converts awareness into urgency: the moment a participant moves from “interesting” to “this is directly relevant to my organisation.”

EXTRAPOLATING (Where · Locate Hot Zones): Where do the leverage zones and burning platforms appear across people, processes, and systems in this unit? With urgency established, participants are guided to locate the specific pressure points within their own organisation where the unit is most exposed. This is a structured diagnostic that surfaces the specific people, processes, and structural conditions that are most vulnerable. Extrapolating turns intelligence into a map of strategic exposure.

CONVERGING ZONE (Collective · Collective Intelligence of Execution; Section 5 · Integration in this unit): What does each executive leadership role contribute? Where does cross-functional insight synthesise in this unit? This stage brings all executive perspectives into dialogue. Participants, operating in assigned executive leadership (CXO) roles, synthesise their individual diagnoses into a single integrated enterprise view. This is where the programme’s defining outcome is produced: the capacity to hold a whole-system perspective, seeing through every window simultaneously.
The arc is repeated across every unit in the programme. The content changes. The discipline of the sequence stays the same.

12: Bridge from 2.2 (between the first two content paragraphs above): Strategy is a collective process. This is where a new layer of complexity emerges.
14: The four families: Each family represents a distinct way in which judgement can become systematically skewed. Within each family sit more specific, observable micro-biases that appear in everyday strategic decisions.
Additional research detail for the biases on this slide:
Illusion of Control: Langer (1975) demonstrated the illusion across high-stakes decision contexts.
Planning Fallacy: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) showed plans consistently ignore base rates of comparable projects.
Loss Aversion: Leads to under-investment in emerging opportunities.
Endowment Effect: Thaler (1980) showed people demand more to give up what they own than they would pay to acquire it.
15: Additional research detail for the biases on this slide:
Career-Risk Bias: Psychological safety research (Edmondson, 1999) shows its pervasive effect on option quality in teams.
Groupthink: Janis (1972) documented groupthink in high-stakes government and corporate decisions.

Key sources with their titles: Kahneman & Tversky (1974, 1979): Heuristics and Biases; Prospect Theory. Kahneman (2011): Thinking, Fast and Slow. Janis (1972): Victims of Groupthink. Christensen (1997): The Innovator’s Dilemma. Rosenzweig (2007): The Halo Effect. Edmondson (1999): Psychological Safety. Page (2007): The Difference.
16: Where functional bias shows up: While functional bias does not appear on any dashboard, it shows up everywhere: in delayed decisions, in misaligned KPIs, in teams working hard in different directions. This is because each executive function experiences the organisation through the variable they control most directly. In an executive performance discussion, functional bias reveals itself in how leaders interpret data, assign causes, and propose remedies.
When asked to describe the “elephant”, they will instinctively describe the dimension of reality their role is trained to notice.
Why the cost compounds: If behavioural biases were merely random fluctuations, they could be treated as statistical noise. They are systematic, so the distortion accumulates.
18: Setting up the illustration: Every executive in the room hears the same words. They do not hear the same message. The illustration demonstrates how functional bias appears in a real executive context.
Imagine a major hospital chain announcing a bold new vision. The vision is clear. Around the table, the mental maths looks very different.

Now imagine that the results after six months show the following: the spike in ‘panic visits’ and the fall in Customer Satisfaction (NPS) described above.
21: Where leaders usually locate bias: Most leaders, when introduced to cognitive bias, instinctively locate it in a person. They think of the overconfident executive, the risk-averse board member, or the team that falls too easily into groupthink. This is a natural but ultimately limited frame.
22: Why the moments matter: Each moment where human judgement is required creates a distinct opening through which systematic distortion can enter and compound. Understanding the map of those moments is the prerequisite for doing anything useful about it.

The four phases: A strategy management process, at its most fundamental, moves through four distinct phases. Each phase asks something different of the people involved: different cognitive demands, different social dynamics, different pressures. Each phase, as a consequence, activates a different cluster of biases.

The four phases are not sequential in any neat sense. In practice they loop, overlap, and revisit. Analytically, they provide a clear structure for understanding where and how distortion enters, and what it costs when it does.
Overview of the four phases (dominant biases; primary risk; what it looks like):
Diagnosis: Availability, Anchoring, Confirmation; wrong reality enters the strategy; analysis confirms what leadership already believes.
Option / Choice Generation: Status Quo, Groupthink, Career-Risk, Silo; solution space is narrowed before debate; only incremental options reach the table.
Decision: Overconfidence, Loss Aversion, Authority, Halo Effect; chosen path is flawed or skewed; the chosen option reflects who proposed it more than what the evidence supports.
Execution: Planning Fallacy, Incentive, Self-Interest; strategy decays in delivery; reporting looks green while results slip red.

Phase 1 · Diagnosis, the combined effect: The diagnosis a leadership team constructs is a filtered, framed, and selectively weighted version of reality, one that typically reflects what the organisation already believed going in.

Phase 2 · Option Generation, how the phase opens: The diagnostic work, however flawed, eventually produces a shared enough view of the situation that a team can turn to the question of options. What could the organisation do? What directions are available? What choices exist?
Further detail on the Phase 2 biases:
Status Quo Bias, the result: The organisation focuses on improving what it has, and rethinking what it could become is left undone.
Functional and Silo Bias: The commercial team sees commercial options. The operations team sees operational ones.
Career-Risk Bias: The radical options are those that challenge inherited assumptions or that could fail conspicuously.
23: Phase 3 · Decision, how the moment looks: A decision has been made. A direction has been chosen. From the outside, it looks like the point where careful thinking and good judgement come together: where the analysis is done, options have been reviewed, and leaders commit to a path. From the inside, it is often the moment when the strongest biases show up.
Further detail on the Phase 3 biases:
Loss Aversion: The organisation consistently chooses the safer path because losses feel more vivid than equivalent gains.
Authority Bias and the Halo Effect: Other voices, however analytically sound, adjust toward the dominant signal.
The Sunk-Cost Fallacy and the Endowment Effect: Existing commitments, current assets, and inherited strategies carry an invisible premium.
High pressure to commit and low tolerance for challenge: those two conditions together create the most fertile ground for bias.

Phase 4 · Execution, why the risk continues: Leaders often assume that biases were part of thinking and ended there. Execution requires something different from planning. Staying aligned, reporting honestly, and recognising quickly when things need to change are exactly the areas where biases tend to show up most strongly, making execution harder than expected.
Further detail on the Phase 4 biases:
The Planning Fallacy: Organisations discover the undercooked plan in delivery, at which point the cost of correction is significantly higher.

Confirmation Bias in its action-reinforcing form: This is what makes the Planning Fallacy so persistent. As execution begins and early signals emerge, the team filters incoming information through what it wants to see. The plan was right; external conditions are the problem.

Incentive Bias: The strategy commits the organisation to certain priorities. The incentive structures that govern individual and team behaviour were designed around different priorities, often last year’s, or the year before.
Self-Interest and Functional Bias: Each function executes its part. Each team pursues its KPIs. Horizontal coordination also runs against the grain of how most leaders are measured.
24: How strategic closure forms: The less responsive organisation starts to overlook important external signals, and avoids questioning its own assumptions and decisions.

The open climate: When leaders are open to input, willing to be challenged, and curious about different perspectives, the organisation strengthens its ability to recognise change, reassess its thinking, and adjust direction when needed. This allows the organisation to adapt effectively while maintaining momentum in execution.
25: From climate to state of being: To make emotional climate actionable, it must move from an abstract organisational condition to something leaders can see, name, and work with directly at the individual level. This shift happens through emotional alignment: the practice of identifying the specific state of being through which strategy is being experienced.

In practice, this means: identifying the prevailing emotional state at leadership and team level; understanding how that state is shaping behaviour and attention; agreeing on behavioural guardrails to stabilise execution under that emotional load.
30: How the practices are organised: by domain (In the Strategy Room, In Leadership Culture). Each practice is a piece of Behavioural Infrastructure (the “System 2” Protocol), paired with its intent: which bias is neutralised.
37: The tool: Behavioural Strategy Leadership Assessment (The Five Commitments · Self-Scoring Tool), an assessment of behaviourally strategy-literate leadership.

How to use this assessment (remaining instructions): Read each statement carefully. Score yourself honestly on a scale of 1 to 5. Avoid scoring what you aspire to. The statements are intentionally broad: each one is designed to apply across the full range of leadership situations you encounter, including and beyond formal strategy moments.
Record your score beside each statement, total each commitment, and transfer the totals to the scoring summary.
38: Scoring summary: Transfer your commitment totals, add them together, then read your interpretation and per-commitment guidance. The summary lists each commitment with its score out of 20 and a “Notes / priorities” column, then the overall total out of 100.
Emerging Awareness (25–44), one further line: This is valuable and honest information.
Per-commitment interpretation: Use your individual commitment scores (each out of 20) alongside the guide below to identify your highest-leverage development priorities.
C1 · I Know My Biases
17–20: Strong self-awareness of your own thinking patterns. Sustain it by building in active reflection at key moments: before a significant call as well as after one has gone wrong.

11–16: Developing awareness. The concepts are clear; the gap is in consistent application under pressure or when pace is high. Identify one recurring context where your thinking patterns are most likely to go unexamined, and focus your attention there first.

4–10: Limited current practice. A useful starting point is building a personal inventory of your known thinking tendencies, ideally with honest input from people who observe you regularly in moments that matter.
C2 · I Manage My Emotional Impact

17–20: High awareness of the climate you create. The most demanding test of this commitment is whether you maintain it when you feel most strongly about an outcome: when the stakes are personal and the pressure is high.

11–16: Awareness is present but likely inconsistent, particularly under pressure or when the outcome matters most to you. Identify one regular setting where you know your presence tends to narrow the thinking in the room, and experiment with a different approach.

4–10: The climate you set may be inadvertently suppressing honest input from those around you. This is among the highest-leverage commitments for leaders in senior roles. Direct feedback from people who work closely with you is the most useful starting point.
C3 · I Build Psychological Safety Deliberately

17–20: Psychological safety appears to be a genuine feature of your leadership environment. Test its depth: does challenge persist when you are under pressure, or when a direction is already in motion? Consistency in those moments is the real measure.

11–16: Safety exists in principle but may be conditional on circumstances. Review whether challenge is structurally enabled, or whether it depends on individual courage in the moment. Design tends to outlast intention.

4–10: The conditions for honest challenge are likely underdeveloped. This is usually a design issue. Structural practices (building in challenge as a role, separating input from decision, creating anonymous channels) tend to be more durable than relying on culture alone.
C4 · I Use Process to Protect Quality

17–20: Process discipline is embedded in your practice. The priority is ensuring it holds under time pressure and high stakes: the precise conditions under which structured thinking is most often abandoned and most needed.

11–16: You apply structured approaches selectively. Identify the moments where you revert most readily to unassisted instinct: these are your highest-exposure points and the most productive focus for development.

4–10: Significant calls are likely being made without sufficient protection against predictable thinking errors. Introducing even one deliberate pressure-testing practice into how you approach your next consequential moment will generate visible benefit.
C5 · I Treat People as the Strategy

17–20: You treat the quality of collective thinking as a resource to be actively invested in. Extend this approach to settings and conversations you design for others, as well as those you are personally involved in.

11–16: Awareness is present; intentional investment in the quality of thinking may be inconsistent. Review how much of your leadership attention goes to developing how your team thinks together, versus reviewing what they produce.

4–10: Energy is likely concentrated on outputs (what is decided, delivered, or reported), with less going to the thinking conditions that produce them. Sustained quality in either requires investing in the latter. This is the commitment that, when underdeveloped, constrains all the others.
